newsitem.title: ITALY: Alitalia unions attack EU stance on restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Alitalia unions attack EU stance on restructuring.

text.p: Unions at Alitalia said on Thursday they were "deeply worried" about the conditions being imposed on the Italian flag carrier in return for European Commission approval of a restructuring plan.
Unions said after a meeting with management that the Commission was demanding a big reduction in the size of the Alitalia fleet, more cost cuts and a smaller than expected injection of fresh funds.

"Unions believe the attitude of Brussels towards Alitalia is deeply prejudiced...and we call on all political forces to strongly back (Alitalia)," the airline's eight unions said in a joint statement.

Debt-riddled Alitalia has requested Commission clearance for a recapitalisation plan worth 3.0 trillion lire ($1.8 billion). The government last week approved the legislation needed to hand state-controlled Alitalia 1.5 trillion lire of this cash.

The European Commission has not yet publicly pronounced on the Alitalia restructuring plan and Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said earlier this week that the EU would study details of the project by the end of March.
But unions said the Alitalia management had told them of initial Commission reaction, including a call for the planned capital increase to be cut to 2.8 trillion lire.

"We're worried that the Commission is asking for cuts to our routes and staff force that we will not be able to support," said Silvano Barberini, an official with the FIT-CISL union, who did not go into further detail.

Alitalia is expected to post losses of around 1.3 trillion lire in 1996 -- its ninth consecutive year in the red -- with restructuring costs of some 800 billion lire weighing heavily on the bottom line.
Alitalia management was locked in bitter conflict with unions for more than a year over plans to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

A truce was finally called last June when labour leaders agreed to a rescue package which allowed for between 20-30 percent of the group's shares to be reserved for employees after the firm's recapitalisation and eventual privatisation. ($ = 1705 Italian Lire)
